title: Contraction
hookLine: Luria taught that God withdrew to make room for a world

cards: Before anyone new can sit at a crowded table, somebody has to scoot over. A small thing. A chair pulled back, a bag moved, an elbow tucked in.

The table doesn't grow. The people already at it draw in a little. In the town of Safed, a teacher named Isaac Luria, whom his students called the Ari, asked something like it about everything there is.
If God is without end and fills all things, where was there room for a world? His answer begins with a drawing in.

teach.b: Tzimtzum. The Hebrew means a contraction, a narrowing, a drawing in. Luria's teaching reaches us through his student Chaim Vital, in a work called Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life.
Before anything was made, Vital writes, the light of the Infinite, the Ein Sof we met not long ago, filled everything. There was no empty space at all. Nowhere for a world to be.

Second, the withdrawing. So the Infinite drew itself in, away from a center, and left an open space: a place where something other than God could exist. In this picture, creation starts with a stepping back.
Into that open space, Vital writes, came a single line of light, reaching in from the Infinite. The space is never cut off. Whatever lives there is held by that thread.

teach.h: READ AS LEAVING, OR AS HIDING.
teach.b: Later teachers disagreed about how to read this. Some took the withdrawal at its word.
Others, Hasidic teachers among them, said God never truly leaves any place, and the contraction is a hiding, so the world can have a place of its own.
Both readings keep a God who makes space rather than taking it all. And some readers hear a human echo in it. A parent who goes quiet so a child can try.
A teacher who leaves a question open. A friend who lets you finish your own sentence.

how: Tzimtzum is studied in Lurianic Kabbalah through Chaim Vital's Etz Chaim and its commentaries, and Hasidic teachers return to it often, especially in discussions of how God can be everywhere and a world can still exist.

o: a burst of light that fills an empty space
a vow to give up something you love
a drawing in, to leave room for something else

s: in Luria's picture, creation begins by pushing outward
it begins with a drawing in, which leaves an open space.
Luria's teaching reaches us through his student Chaim Vital
Vital set it down in Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life.
every teacher reads the contraction literally
later teachers disagreed; some Hasidic teachers read it as a hiding, not a leaving.

games.q: you are the Infinite, and you fill everything. there's no room for a world. what does Luria's teaching say happens?
o: the Infinite draws in and leaves an open space.
the world is made somewhere outside God.
games.why: creation starts with a withdrawing: the Infinite draws in, and a single line of light reaches into the space left open.

practice: Bring to mind one person who could use a little more space from you: maybe you talk over them, fix things before they've asked, or fill every silence.
Picture the next time you're together, and see yourself leaving a pause, not walking away, just drawing in a little so there's room.
Rest there, and notice what might grow in that space: their words, their idea, their own way of doing it.

wordCard.voice: Tzimtzum. Contraction: in Luria's teaching, the Infinite drawing in to leave room for a world. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: make room. Creation, in this picture, starts with a stepping back. See you tomorrow.
